I will now make a statement as the President of the General Assembly. Excellencies, Mr. Secretary-General, Under-Secretary, esteemed colleagues. Thank you for joining this final briefing on the UN80 Initiative, at least the final briefing for the 80th session and the final briefing over which I will preside. Therefore, I would like to really thank you for the last 10 meetings we had together. And I remember very well around this time last year, everyone was asking me what my priorities in this 80th session would be, which big events I would organize, what I wanted to achieve during my presidency, and I said UN80. Frankly speaking, most of the people outside of the house did not understand what I was talking about, and maybe also some inside thought, but this is not really fancy, but I deeply believe that these fragmented times mean nothing fancy, but rather to really focus on the core of this institution, especially in a time under pressure. We, alongside with the selection process of the Secretary General, therefore underline that the UN80 initiative has been our priority. Because if we are not reforming ourselves, meaning less bureaucracy, more efficiency, we cannot protect it against the attacks we have dramatically seen over the year, not only by breaching the Charter, but also by heavy financial cuts. In pushing forward with the UNAD reforms, we choose to make some difficult but necessary decisions to strengthen this organization and equip it for the future. And for that, dear colleagues, I commend each and every one of you. In total, we held 10 briefings throughout the session, offering us an opportunity to dive into the interfaces and nuances of each three work streams. And today, I'm pleased to say that we have driven meaningful progress across each of the three. Under work stream one, we advanced targeted post reduction for the program budget, delivering a revised 2026 budget in line with the Secretary-General's revised estimates. We moved forward on consolidated common administration platforms and addressed financial credit return and clawback mechanisms with the aim of redirecting resources towards core delivery. Throughout Work Stream 2, the adoption of the landmark Mandate Resolution introduced greater discipline into the mandate lifecycle, moving us away from the endless creation of new mandates and towards a more systematic process of reviewing those already in place. All of this has been supported by the practical tools adopted, including UN80 Action Dashboard, the Mended Registry, and the Transparency Gateway, as well as time limits through microphone cutoff and streamlining our committee work and agendas. And I would especially like to thank the co-facilitators, one of them is here today, for this incredible work. And on a work from three, we tackled perhaps the most difficult question of all. how the institutional architecture of the United Nations itself can be reformed and refitted to better serve the people who depend upon it. The SGs regular briefings gave the membership an opportunity to engage directly with major institutional evaluations, including shifting paradigms, united to deliver, and to consider concrete proposals relating to UN country team configurations, regional resets, and stronger cross-pillar coordination. We've also advanced structural changes, including the merger of the United Nations system staff colleague and UNITAR, bringing together two capacity building bodies. And we know that this is also the discussion ground for further mergers. And as there have been some comments and debates this morning when we decided on this important resolution, I would just like to underline that so far in the process, we work very closely together between the SG's office and the OPGA with all the member states, but especially also with all the boards of the different institutions. So the process started way before we took the action in the General Assembly. It started spring and followed over the early summer months. All these successes we have done together in all three work groups, they may sound like technical changes, budgets, mandates, dashboards, institutional configurations, but behind each of them are months of hard work, detailed negotiations, and effective diplomacy. And together, they represent something much bigger, an organization willing to examine itself honestly, to make difficult choices, and to be ready to change. But celebration cannot be complacency. And I want to be frank and honest as I'm leaving this office in a couple of days. Over the year, when we were discussing and looking at the reform steps, especially also right before Christmas in the Fifth Committee, I think we are just in the midst of this reform. And we should not avoid the edges which we still have to face. Because when cutting, especially under work stream one, And looking in the budget review, which is upcoming in fall again, there's still the elephant in the room, the big strategic political debate about the whole setup of the different mandates, but especially about the different structures in this house. With more than 200 USGs and ASG level posts across the US system, we must ask more fundamental question about duplication, mandates, and whether our structures remain fit for the purpose. And this can only work if member states engage. So these 10 meetings were meant also as a preparation for engagement, not only here, USPRs who attended many of the meetings, but also the missions and whole government approaches. Clearly, this also underlines that UNAD is not finished in the 80th session. Indeed, in many respects, the most difficult work still lies ahead, and these reforms will continue under the stewardship of my successor, to whom I wish all the best, and we work closely together in the transition phase, and above, in all your hands as a membership within the 81st session. We all know none of this will be easy, but as I have said before, the United Nations was not created for the easy times. It was created exactly for moments like this, when it needed people to stand up and take leadership, take responsibility. And in this regard, I would like to thank, especially you personally, dear Secretary General, and also Under-Secretary General Guy Ryder, for taking this UN-AID initiative even way before the AIDS session, for standing up, for facing the many questions or even headwinds. when you put on the table that this institution deeply has to reform. And I would like to thank also those during this session who fully embraced this process, especially but not only the co-chairs of Workstream 2, many PRs here, but also so many team members, experts in your missions. Because we have also seen over the course of this year that even as everyone is calling for change, when the moment for change actually comes, maybe it's human nature, and perhaps even more diplomatic nature, it is often pushed back again to avoid any ripples or controversy. But at a time when our house is under attack, we do not have the luxury of being bystanders. We have to take the future into our hands, and that means taking reform into our hands. So let's keep going, even in the last three days of this 80th session and even more in the next 81st session. I wish you all the best for that UNAT reform. Dear Secretary General, please, the floor is yours.

Madam President, Excellencies, Distinguished Delegates, Let me begin by thanking you, Madam President, for your leadership throughout the 80th session, for keeping the UNAT initiative firmly on the agenda and for creating regular opportunities for frank, constructive intergovernmental dialogue. As your presidency draws to a close, I want to recognize your stewardship and sustained commitment. Excellencies, I launched the UN80 Initiative out of a profound sense of responsibility. Responsibility to the people the United Nations serves, responsibility to future generations, responsibility to this Assembly, which has entrusted us with mandates of extraordinary importance and responsibility to this Organization. The case for the UN80 remains clear. The world is demanding more from the United Nations, even as conflict is spreading, humanitarian needs are multiplying, development gains are under pressure, and trust is being tested. We are answering that call with real change. strengthening mandate delivery, reducing fragmentation, sharpening accountability, and ensuring the resources entrusted to us yield the greatest possible impact for those we serve. Throughout, the Sustainable Development Goals have remained our North Star, and the Pact for the Future, our political compass. UNHAT is helping us better equip the system to deliver both. Excellencies, UNIT was launched less than 18 months ago. We have since moved from diagnosis to design and increasingly implementation. Not everything is moving at the same speed, not truth it. Some changes fall within my authority and are already being implemented. Some require decisions by this Assembly or other governing bodies. And some require further analysis and consultation before decisions can be taken. But across the three work streams of UNHAT, the direction of travel is increasingly clear. First, we are changing how the organization uses its resources and manages its operations. Work stream one began with an urgent task to find efficiencies and improvements within existing mandates. That work is already reshaping the Secretariat's operating model. The 2026 changes include a 21% reduction in posts in the Secretariat, relocation of functions to lower-cost locations, and efforts across the system to consolidate services and eliminate duplication. By spending less on unnecessary administrative and bureaucratic processes, we can do more on what matters most. mandate delivery, and impact. That same logic is driving the move towards shared services. A common administrative platform in New York now serves approximately 6,000 personnel. Payroll functions have been consolidated into a single global team. A digital hub has been launched in Valencia. And in July, we published the Unified Services Roadmap A framework for examining how operational services can be shared across entities, pillars and locations. The feasibility analysis foresees efficiencies of 20 to 80% in various back office services. But this must be made real before the resources, time and capacity they save can be redirected towards delivery. Technology and data are part of the same transformation. The technology-accelerated platform is helping us move from fragmented solutions towards common approaches. The UN System Data Commons has begun bringing data and statistics from across the system into a single platform. With commitments from more than 25 UN entities, it will go live in the coming weeks. where we perform essentially the same function, We should ask whether we truly need separate systems, separate platforms, and separate infrastructure, and we should act accordingly. Second, we have made important breakthroughs on mandates. For decades, mandates have accumulated faster than they have been systematically managed and reviewed. General Assembly resolution 80/251 gives us a new way to address this challenge, while reaffirming the principle that decisions on mandates are the exclusive prerogative of Member States. The role of the United Nations is to implement those mandates, delivering on your decisions as effectively and efficiently as possible. But there should be a clear line connecting mandates, resources, implementation, results and review. This infrastructure is being built to enable Member States to be the most effective and informed custodians of mandates across their life cycle. The Mandate Registry brings together over 40,000 resolutions and decisions dating back to 1946, and links them to programmes, budget references and Secretary-General's reports. We have reviewed more than 600 series of mandated Secretary-General's reports, issued over the past three years. New guidance is making them shorter, clearer, more evidence-based, and more action-oriented. If fully implemented, the initial changes could reduce reporting by about 700,000 words this year alone. That's longer than the novel War and Peace. Which means that in our reports, at least, peace is finally winning out. The significance of these changes goes well beyond word counts. We are also establishing a robust focal point network to assist Member States throughout the resolution process, and developing better digital tools for delegates, including a mobile application to help you navigate meetings, documents and contacts. This infrastructure provides Member States with better information with which to govern. Clearer mandates, clearer responsibilities, clearer links to resources, and clearer evidence of results. And the work underway in the ad hoc working group, including on criteria and modalities for reviewing mandates, can help resolution 1820/51 serve as a lasting instrument of disciplined governance. Third, we are beginning to change how the United Nations system is organized to deliver. This is perhaps the most ambitious dimension of UNHAT. Under the new Humanitarian Compact, we are testing a new model of humanitarian delivery and piloting it in some of the world's most demanding operating environments: Afghanistan, Haiti, Somalia, Sudan, and the Occupied Palestinian Territory. Humanitarian planning simplified. Supply chains integrated. Data systems connected. Roles and responsibilities clarified. And Resident and Humanitarian Coordinators given stronger tools to bring teams together around common priorities and accountability. The aim is to reach people faster, reduce duplications, and use scarce humanitarian resources where needs are greatest. We are also taking reforms of the UN development system to the next level. Country teams are moving towards configurations more responsive to national needs and priorities. The ECOSOC resolution on progress in the implementation of the quadriennial comprehensive policy review provides critical guidance as we advance this work. The expertise on demand mechanism is being developed so countries can draw on capacities from across the system even if those capacities are not physically present. The mechanism complements, rather than replaces, sustained country presence. It will bring together a catalogue of expertise, protocols for assessing them easily, and administrative arrangements, building on what already exists, without creating new architecture. This is critical to ensuring the UN's deep technical and normative expertise is available where and when Member States need it, while enabling more tailored and efficient responses to country needs and priorities. A system-wide expertise catalogue, instruments and protocols are due to launch by the High-Level Week. Joint Knowledge Hubs are pooling knowledge on key themes. The Regional Platforms for Integration will bring together capacities across UN pillars and deepen support to the country level. And the Shared Platform Initiative is strengthening the ability of Resident and Humanitarian Coordinators to ensure more coherent support to interrelated humanitarian and development functions. Ultimately, it will help bring the UN system together around common priorities and results, and it responds to specific challenges in countries. The Resident Coordination System is also pursuing recalibration to ensure it is optimally configured to further deliver on Member States' expectations. This will also be critical to ensure effective delivery of all UNAT measures unfolding at country level. Together, these improvements can put us on a stronger footing to navigate financial constraints, deliver through 2030, and help shape the sustainable development framework that will carry us beyond it. Excellencies, we are also stressing coherence across substantive pillars of our work. The Human Rights Group is providing a stronger mechanism for UN system-wide coordination. In peace and security, the recent review of the future of all forms of UN peace operations examines how our toolbox can better match today's conflict landscape. It puts greater emphasis on prevention, political solutions, peacebuilding, more focused mandates, stronger partnerships, and more flexible mission models. And calls for the best-equipped entities to perform mandated programmatic tasks with the corresponding resources. Across the system, we are looking at whether institutional arrangements remain fit for purpose. This includes the structural proposals attracting significant attention, including your action earlier today. I welcome your decision this morning to merge the United Nations System Staff College and UNITAR. This will bring together complementary capacities to provide stronger training services for Member States and UN system personnel. This decision is an important step forward for the UN80 initiative, and I am glad it was approved during the General Assembly's 80th session. It is part of the broader consolidation of the UN system's training and research capacities. An implementation roadmap for integrating UNRISD, the UN Research Institute for Social Development, into the UN University has been endorsed by the two entities concerned. This will ensure the continuity of UNRIS research while bringing it within UNU's institutional framework, establish UNRIS as a UNU institute. We also have a clear roadmap for integration of the UN Interregional Crime and Justice Research Institute into UNODC, uniting their complementary strengths to deliver more effective support on crime prevention and justice. UNITAR and UNU are developing a mechanism to improve coordination of training and research activities across the wider UN system and translate knowledge more effectively into practice for Member States. Potential benefits of a merger between UNDP and UNOPS are being discussed in the context of the Executive Board of UNDP, UNFPA, UNOPS, and terms of reference for an independent assessment are being prepared. The two entities are exploring measures to enhance coherence, coordination and efficiency. The strategic assessment concerning UNFPA and UN Women has examined the potential of bringing complementary capacities together to best support women, girls and youth. This could consolidate expertise on gender equality and women's rights with expertise on sexual and reproductive health and rights, population dynamics and young people. The two Executive Directors have presented detailed analyses to their respective Boards, and I myself have provided in-depth responses to questions from Member States and the Boards about the implications of a possible merger. We will carefully consider the next steps, taking into account the results obtained by the Boards. Meanwhile, Work on progressively transitioning global and country-level functioning of UNAIDS to other parts of the UN system is advancing, with concrete decisions expected in October. An information brief on the internal review of arrangements for the UN system's work on the environment will also be presented to Member States this month. On every front. We are exploring where deeper integration, program realignment or structural change can improve impact and institutional integrity. That is exactly how UN80 should work. Start with the problem, follow the evidence, focus on the mandate, and choose the institutional solution that delivers greatest impact. Excellencies, the first phase of UN80 was about identify possibilities, the second was about testing them, building the evidence and defining pathways. We have now entered the third phase about decisions and implementation. Moving from pilots to scale. The lessons from the new Humanitarian Compact's five pilot settings must inform wider humanitarian operations. Shared services must move from feasibility studies and roadmaps to measurable implementation. Country team reconfiguration, regional platforms for integration, expertise on demand, and knowledge hubs must bring changes people and governments can see and feel and benefit from. Technology and data platforms must become generally shared tools. And the work on funding mechanisms must make core and pool funding more effective and attractive, improve the quality of earmarked funding, and strengthening the funding compact. And system-wide results management must strengthen the connection between mandates, resources and results without creating more bureaucracy. Above all, Member States will be in the driver's seat. Many of the decisions ahead do not belong to the Secretary-General. They belong to you. And that is why coherent actions by the General Assembly and other intergovernmental organs will be decisive. A shared service concept that is supported in principle but lets entities easily opt out, will not produce efficiency. A country-level model designed around national priorities will not succeed if funding incentives continue to reward separate institutional footprints and projects disconnected from our collective support for country needs. The principle of national ownership must be fully respected. And mandates cannot be made more disciplined if each negotiation adds requirements without considering the cumulative task. The next phase of UNAT is mainly about changing behaviour across the Secretariat, across the system, and across intergovernmental bodies. Excellencies, my progress report in May spelled out six asks of Member States. They are just as relevant today. First, Use resolution 80/251 as a governance tool. Apply it as a strategic instrument across the full mandate life cycle, from creation to resourcing, implementation, assessment and review. The Secretariat will provide the tools and information, but only Member States can take decisions on mandates. Second, support our efforts to deliver on your guidance concerning new country and regional arrangements. Help us ensure that the reconfiguration of UN country teams is delivered in countries in full consultation with those governments. Continue to guide the reset of the regional architecture in the General Assembly this fall. And ensure the recalibrated Resident Coordinator system has the adequate and predictable financing needed to fulfill the role Member States have asked it to perform. We opened the way with a robust ECOSOC resolution Now you can finish the job. Third, back us on shared services, technology and data to improve delivery. Help us make joint solutions the default wherever they provide better quality, greater efficiency and more transparency. Use our role in governing bodies to challenge duplication and support common standards and platforms. Fourth, Consider structural proposals on their merits. Judge merger, consolidation and transition proposals by the evidence. Ask whether they protect mandates, improve delivery, reduce unnecessary fragmentation and boost impact. Then take decisions through the applicable rules, procedures and governing bodies. Fifth, align funding practices with UNHCR objectives. Funding choices shape institutional behaviour. Support adequate core resources, effective pooled funding, and higher quality earmarked funding that encourages collaboration, not competition. And pay assessed contributions in full and on time, without conditions or delay. Efficiency can make every dollar work harder, it cannot make an unpaid dollar appear. Six, exercise governance coherently across the United Nations system. carry the objectives of UN80 consistently across the General Assembly and other governing bodies, because coherent governance is what makes coherent delivery possible.

Excellencies, when I launched UN80, I spoke of responsibility. I return to that particular word today because, ultimately, responsibility is what will determine whether this initiative succeeds. In the coming months, I intend to use every day I have available to push this work forward, to consolidate the changes underway, to advance the reforms that still need to be done, and to ensure that the momentum we have created is transformed into lasting change. The true measure of UN80 will be whether, a few years down the line, this organization works differently, because of the choices we're making today. And, above all, whether the people we serve notice that the United Nations responds quicker and more efficiently, acts more coherently and delivers more effectively. As we head into the 81st session, I urge Member States to not merely maintain the momentum of UN80, but to deepen it. to take the decisions that are ready to be taken, to use the tools we've crafted, to demand evidence of results being achieved, to match mandates with the means to deliver on them, and to reward collaboration rather than fragmentation, and to carry these principles consistently across every governing body of this organization. 80 years ago, our predecessors built the United Nations because they understood that a difficult world required institutions capable of rising to the occasion. That responsibility now falls to us. Our task is to bequeath a United Nations that is stronger than when we found it, an organization that is more coherent in the way it works, more disciplined in how it uses its resources, and better equipped to fulfill the promises made in its name. That is the opportunity we have before us. There's a lot of work ahead. Together, we must see it through.

I thank you. I thank the Secretary-General for the comprehensive report. I now give the floor to the co-chair of the ad hoc working group on mandate implementation review and permanent representative of Norway.

Thank you, President, Secretary-General. Ambassador Wallace and I have the honor to brief you in our capacity as co-chairs of the ad hoc working group on mandate implementation review and pursuant to General Assembly resolution 80/251, provide the Assembly with an update on the progress of the working group at the end of the 80th session. The Secretary-General's UN80 initiative continues to guide our collective effort to strengthen the effectiveness, efficiency and coherence of the United Nations. Attention to mandate creation, implementation and review remain one of the central work streams of that initiative, and we are grateful for the sustained energy that Member States have brought to this task. Within this session, resolution 80/251 set out four specific deliverables for the working group under paragraph 33. Developing templates and model clauses, by the end of May 2026; consideration of the review of mandated reports by the end of July 2026; and development of criteria and modalities to guide decisions on the renewal, adaptation, merger, replacement or retirement of General Assembly mandates by the end of August. President, we are grateful for this opportunity to report to the Assembly today on our progress against each deliverable. President and dear colleagues, as called for under paragraph 33d of the resolution, on 29 May 2026, we have the honour to transmit to Member States finalized concept note, resolution and decision templates, and model mandate implementation review and retirement clauses. These tools are intended to help Member States implement our agreement in resolution 80/251. to provide concise concept notes for new mandates and to include mandate implementation review clauses in all new and renewing mandates. They reflect the sustained input of Member States and close consultation with the Secretariat. We remain grateful to all who contributed. Delegations have been encouraged to use and adapt those tools for new or renewing resolutions initiated from 1 June and onwards. We were very pleased that the first concept note making use of them was submitted within days of their circulation. We wish to underline, as we did at the time, that the templates are offered as reference tools rather than rigid formats, recognising that no single approach will fit every mandate. Proponents remain free to adapt the model language or to draft new clauses to suit circumstances that the templars do not anticipate, or simply to fit the unique context of each mandate. Pursuant to paragraph 16 of resolution 8251, The Secretariat was requested to review the full portfolio of the Secretary-General's mandated reports and to identify candidates for combination or a change in periodicity, for presentation to Member States by the end of June this year. The Secretariat's note to this end was circulated at the end of June. We convened the working group on 16 July to consider the draft. The secretariat outlined practical improvements that it intends to apply from September onwards across its reporting, including concise update reports where there has been no material change, clearer word limits and greater use of data and visual presentation. The secretariat also advised that specific recommendations arising from their reporting review would be brought forward when individual mandates come up for consideration or renewal in the respective mandating bodies. For us, as member states, receiving and putting these recommendations into action will be a key task in the upcoming committee season. And with that, I pass the floor to Brian.

Thank you, Despina. We need co-chairs. Madam President, Secretary-General, Excellencies, colleagues, paragraphs 33 D, Roman 3 and 4 of resolution 8251 task the working group with developing, respectively, clear and objective criteria to guide decisions on the renewal, adaptation, merger, replacement or retirement of General Assembly mandates, and modalities to guide the review of the existing stock of such mandates. Given how closely related these two deliverables are, we chose to pursue them in tandem. From an initial exchange of views on 2 June, we circulated a non-paper on 12 June, and held hybrid workshops on 16 and 18 June, followed by a working group meeting on 16 July. We are truly grateful to the many delegations who engaged with us in the room on those occasions, as well as through written submissions. All of those inputs culminated in a report of the co-chairs on criteria and modalities, which we circulated on 14 August. The report consolidates the inputs and reflections received into a practical framework, comprising agreed principles to be applied as criteria to guide Member States in assessing mandates, and a menu of flexible review modalities. We wish to stress that, as the report itself makes clear, that it is offered as guidance rather than as a set of prescriptive requirements. and that no single criterion is intended to determine an outcome for any individual mandate. On criteria, the report sets out nine principles drawn from paragraph 1 of the resolution and from the understandings reached in our consultations. Building on those principles, The report proposes three core criteria for Member States to consider when assessing a mandate for renewal, adaptation, merger, replacement or retirement. Namely, whether the objectives have been achieved, the impact of its implementation, and its coherence with related mandates. And together with supporting considerations covering the mandate's original design, its implementation status, its reporting requirements, duplication or fragmentation, and its resourcing. A checklist reflecting these criteria is also annexed to the report as a practical tool for Member States. On modalities, the report reflects the broad convergence we heard that reviews of the existing stock of mandates should be undertaken primarily by the bodies that originated them, consistent with their own working methods, with the working group serving as a forum for coordination and the exchange of lessons learned, rather than as a central review mechanism. The report sets out a menu of modalities for main committees and other bodies to draw upon, including thematic clustering, adjustment of reporting periodicity, and consolidation of related mandates together with continued strengthening of the Mandate Registry as a shared evidence base. To test this framework in practice, we will invite volunteer groupings of Member States to undertake thematic pilot reviews, with the lessons learned informing any further refinement and scaling of review modalities. The report also clarifies that this work will continue to be informed by the Secretary-General's reports requested in resolution 8251. Madam President, Member States have not yet had the opportunity to react to this report in a reconvened meeting of the Working Group, but we intend to ensure that that is taken care of shortly. What we have presented, though, reflects our best efforts as Co-Chairs to consolidate a genuinely broad range of views into a coherent, practical and usable framework. We wish to be clear that this report represents a further step in an ongoing and inclusive process, and not a concluded outcome. It does not prejudge the decisions of Member States, nor constitute the implementation of any review mechanism. We want to take this opportunity to once again thank the Secretariat for briefing the working group throughout the session on the practical tools being developed to support our work, including on the launch of transcripts.un.org and on an expanded mandates.un.org registry, which we have been informed will continue to grow in functionality. The Secretariat has also proposed a technical briefing, and we will announce the timing on that soon. to walk delegations through these tools in greater detail, and we would encourage from you, colleagues, the broadest possible participation. We also take this opportunity to thank you, Madam President of the General Assembly, and your office, as well as the Secretary-General and your Executive Office, and the broader Secretariat, for their unfailing support on both substance and logistics. Our collective work on mandates would not be possible without this support. Madam President, in line with resolution 82/51, we have sought today to give the Assembly an account of where our work stands at this juncture. We remain conscious that the tasks entrusted to us under resolution 82/51 are not yet complete. The resolution envisages that the working group's substantive consideration will continue beyond this session. And if called upon to do so, we intend to use the period ahead to bring the criteria and modalities work to a landing that commands the broadest possible support among member states. Colleagues, your engagement and inputs throughout this period have been thoughtful, constructive, and ambassadors and experts alike have been generous with your time. We take this opportunity to thank you all once again for your continued spirit of collaboration and collegiality. We are committed to carrying the momentum built during the session forward so that the practical improvements we have begun, and in the spirit of partnership that has carried us thus far, continues to deliver tangible results for Member States and for the people the United Nations serves. Thank you, Madam President.

Madam President, Mr. Secretary-General, Excellencies, the European Union welcomes today's briefing on progress under the UN Aid Initiative, a testament to the collective determination to make this organization fit for the challenges of the 21st century. Secretary-General, As we approach the final stretch of your tenure, we should all acknowledge the courage and vision you have brought to this essential reform agenda. The EU remains a steadfast partner in ensuring that UN80 delivers tangible, lasting change, not just for efficiency's sake, but to strengthen trust in multilateralism and among us, and to improve the UN's ability to deliver for people worldwide. Today's discussion takes place against the backdrop of an important deliverable and achievement of the UN reform, the adoption just this morning of the PGA-led resolution to merge UNITAR and UNSSC. This consolidation, preserving the strengths and mandates of both institutions, shows as proof of concept that UNAD works. The EU commends this step and encourages its swift implementation as a springboard for broader change. We appreciate the progress outlined in your report, Mr. Secretary-General, particularly the advances in Workstream 1 on Secretariat efficiencies, and we look forward to further and consequent steps in this direction. Addressing the multiple and interconnected root causes of inefficiency across the UN system, also brings us to the critical work of Workstream 2. We regard the adoption of resolution 80/251 as a significant step forward, providing us with a clear roadmap for change, and warmly welcome the recent update presented by the Co-Chairs on principles for mandate review. The EU has long advocated for a systematic, evidence-based approach across the mandate life cycle to reviewing mandates, ensuring that they remain relevant, coherent and fit for purpose, while addressing mandates that no longer demonstrate clear added value. The principles focused on relevance, coherence and measurable outcomes are a much needed step forward, and we look forward to decisive action in strengthening and streamlining mandates in the immediate future. Progress across the three work streams must be mutually reinforcing. Mandate review should inform structural decisions and resource allocation, while efficiencies and structural reforms should strengthen rather than predetermine or undermine mandate delivery. Let us be clear, UN80 is not just about cutting costs, it is about strengthening the UN's ability to act and deliver. The humanitarian reset, the peace operations review and the push for mandate discipline are not ends in themselves, the means to a more effective United Nations that delivers across peace, security, human rights and sustainable development. And the EU stands ready to support these efforts on these grounds, including through aligned funding, political backing and technical expertise. Colleagues, as we highlight the legacy of the Secretary-General's tenure on this file, Let us also look ahead with ambition, maintaining momentum for reform. The substantial progress made so far demonstrates that change is possible. The Mandate Review Co-Chairs' proposals show that the appetite for reform exists. Now, we must seize this moment and work together to further advance on Work Stream 3 for the system to deliver with more impact on the ground, leaving no one behind. This includes a fit-for-purpose UN reconfiguring and means a more responsive and strategically configured UN country teams led by empowered resident coordinators with strong, coherent cooperation frameworks at their heart, boosting expertise on demand, leveraging regional expertise and undertaking structural reforms where it makes sense. We must ensure that every mandate, every euro, every effort counts. The European Union, in closing, reaffirms its commitment to working with you, with Member States, and with the incoming leadership to turn the promise of UN80 into full reality. Let us build on today's momentum to create a UN that is leaner, more accountable, more coherent, and certainly more effective, one that can rise to the challenges of our time and deliver on the hopes of our people. Thank you.

Thank you, Madam President. I have the honor to speak on behalf of the Group of Least Developed Countries. The LDC group aligns itself with the statement delivered on behalf of the Group of 77 and China. Madam President, as you conclude your tenure next week, the LDC group sincerely commends you for your valuable contribution and steadfast leadership of the General Assembly at a critical moment for multilateralism and the UN itself. The group also thanks the Secretary-General for his important briefing and the co-chairs for their report on criteria and modalities for mandate implementation review, together with the accompanying checklist. We welcome the progress made across three work streams under the UNAT initiative. We particularly welcome the reaffirmation that mandate implementation review must remain fully member state-led. There can be no one-size-fits-all approach. Mandates remain valid until fully implemented. Complementarity must not be confused with duplication, and that weak implementation resulting from under-resourcing should not automatically become grounds for retirement. the group would like to highlight the following. First, development must be placed more clearly at the center of this exercise. It must not be weakened directly or indirectly through mandate consolidation, reduced reporting, or reallocation of resources away from development activities. For LDCs, this is a matter of practical consequence. Our countries account for approximately 13% of the world's population, but only around 1.3% of global GDP. More than 510 million people in LDCs continue to live in extreme poverty. We therefore reiterate that resources Released through very, verified if sense against suit wherever possible, be redeployed to extend on development mandates and operational activities in program countries in accordance with the established intergovernmental and pository processes. Second, the checklist should more fully reflect the qualitative safeguards contained in the report. A finding that a mandate has been only partially implemented, for example, does not explain why. It may reflect inadequate financing, insufficient staffing, weak data, external shocks, limited national capacity, or an absence of international support originally envisaged. The checklist should therefore ask whether the mandate has been adequately resourced, what obstacles have prevented its full implementation, whether those obstacles remain relevant, whether the mandate responds to the needs of structurally vulnerable countries, whether it implements an internationally agreed program of action or a special support measure, and what consequences of its merger, adaptation, or retirement would be for intended beneficiaries. Third, the criteria should include an explicit assessment of equity and differential impact. Relevance, impact, and coherence are useful starting points, but any review must also consider whether a proposed change would disproportionately affect developing countries, particularly LDCs and other countries in special situations. Fourth, thematic clustering and consolidation must not dilute mandates specifically established for LDCs. Similarity in subject matter does not necessarily constitute duplication. A general mandate on development financing, trade, climate action, or capacity building cannot automatically substitute for one addressing the particular vulnerabilities and internationally agreed priorities of LDCs. any proposal to merge, rationalize, or change the periodicity of an LDC relevant mandate should therefore demonstrate that its substantive commitments, dedicated visibility, accountability, and resources will be preserved or strengthened. Fifth, adjustment to reporting periodicity should be approached with care. Before changing a reporting cycle, member states should assess the report's contribution to decision making, monitoring, and accountability, as well as the potential consequences for affected beneficiaries. Sixth, the proposed pilots must be transparent, representative, and without prejudice. These pilots must ensure equitable geographical representation and the meaningful participation of developing countries, including LDCs and other countries in special situations. Pilots should test methodologies, not predetermine political outcomes. Finally, LDC perspectives must be integrated across all three pillars. The Group proposed that every mandate review, regardless of the pillar under which it is classified, includes and assessment of its potential consequences for LDCs and other countries in a special situation. The LDCs should also be meaningfully represented in relevant pilots and consultation across all three pillars where a mandate has a foreseeable impact on LDCs. The LDC groups should be consulted before any recommendation concerning its adaptation, merger, replacement, or retirement is finalized. I thank you.

The work of the group in the weeks ahead is of relevant importance and needs to continue in the most inclusive and transparent manner. I thank you.
I thank the distinguished representative of Egypt, and now I'm going to give the floor to the last speaker in my list, the Republic of Korea.

Thank you, Mr. Chair. The Republic of Korea commends the Secretary-General for his leadership in advancing UNAD initiative from broad proposals toward concrete action. We also appreciate co-chairs of the Ad Hoc Working Group for presenting the report on criteria and modality for mandate implementation review. Important progress has been made across all three work streams. The task force, the task force is now to carry this progress toward and translate it into tangible improvement. Against this backdrop, I'd like to highlight three points. First, we strongly support practical measures that reduce duplicity and consolidate administrative functions and expand the shared services. The Republic of Korea remains committed to working constructively toward this goal. I thank you.
I thank the distinguished representative of the Republic of Korea. Now I give the floor to the Secretary-General to make some observations.

Excellencies, may I first of all thank you for the extremely rich and important debate that is full of considerations that are very important for us as we move on with our work. And I would like to be very clear once again that UNHAT is not a process to replace the Agenda 2030 or the Pact of the Future. On the contrary, UNAT is an instrument in order to make more effective the capacity of the UN to deliver, both in relation to the Agenda 2030 and the Pact of the Future. On the other hand, I also like to say that the objective of UNAT is not to sacrifice the implementation of mandates by reducing resources. The objective of UNHCR is to be more effective and more efficient in order also to better implement the mandates, which are not of our responsibility as Secretariat, that are entirely at the responsibility of the Member States. It's up for the Member States to decide what the mandates are. Our role is to implement them in the most effective way. And one of the objectives of UNHAT is exactly to become more efficient and more effective in implementation of those mandates. I would like to also say that two words that were mentioned many times in this debate have my full agreement, transparency and inclusivity. We did our best to be fully transparent in the preparatory work of UNHCR. It started, of course, with an initial report. After that, other reports were produced. I myself participated in a few of these plenary meetings. My Under Secretary General, Guy Ryder, my colleague, Under Secretary General, has participated in several of these meetings. Members of the agencies went to the respective boards in the discussions that were related to the intervention of those boards. And we were always entirely at the disposal of Member States for any additional meeting, any additional clarification. And we wanted to have full transparency in our work and full inclusivity. In relation, for instance, to the merger of UNITAR and Staff College. Before presenting the proposal to the General Assembly, and then the General Assembly obviously has its own procedures, but before presenting the proposal to the General Assembly, we went to the boards of the two agencies that endorsed that operation. And then we continued a number of other consultations before we thought that we were in a position to present a proposal for member states then to decide according to their own analysis. and their own vision of what should be done. And I also would like to say that when we started this process, I was asked to be bold. And this was said by numerous members of this Assembly. I can tell you that I have no hard feelings if many Member States tell me today not to be as bold as that. And I think that this is normal in any process of decision making when problems become more complicated. But, again, we always acted in full respect of the dialogue with Member States. particularly in the areas that are of intergovernmental decision. Of the 85 actions that are due in 80, 15 were approved in 2026 and they were essentially related to the budget process and the decisions were all intergovernmental. Then, we have presented proposals in relation to 20 actions that are now under intergovernmental processes of different natures, and we are, naturally, in dialogue with the Member States to support the work of the intergovernmental bodies, but the decisions, of course, are strictly of Member States. And in relation to the other 50, that are of the UN system and under my, I would say, coordination, not only there have been many consultations, but we will be presenting briefings about the implementation of those decisions that fall under my responsibility. Of the 50 40 will be included in 20 briefings, of which five will be ready today at the end of business, another five before the UN General Assembly, and the following 10 immediately afterwards. in order to have full information for Member States about all the actions that are taking place under my authority. On the other hand, in relation to the 20 that are now in intergovernmental processes, I will be always, even personally, at the disposal of the intergovernmental bodies for whatever support might be considered necessary. And by the way, in relation to one of the measures that were mentioned, that has to do with the merger of UN Women and UNFPA, not only the two leaders of the agencies have met with the Board and provided the report to the Board, I myself engaged in dialogue with the bureaus of the Board and with several Member States. I received a request with a number of questions and concerns, and I produced myself a very detailed answer Obviously, I fully accept that the Board is not yet in a position to approve the merger, and so we will go on with our dialogue, and I am intending to present several new ideas and proposals for the work of the Board. So, full inclusivity and full cooperation with the intergovernmental bodies. On the other hand, I would like to say that when one looks at the other intergovernmental processes, I have a special word of gratitude to the work of the ECOSOC. The ECOSOC dealt to some of the crucial aspects of the improvement of our work on the fields. in relation to the resident coordination system, in relation to the reconfiguration of country teams, and that is linked also to the regional reset and linked to the expertise on demand. and links to the creation of the hubs, but the truth is that the work of the ECOSOC was extremely important and provided us with an essential guidance in order to implement some of the most relevant aspects of the UNAT. And so I do believe that there has been an interaction between the Member States and the Secretariat that I consider a model, because Member States have been totally committed to these discussions and the Secretariat has done everything possible in order to correspond to the legitimate rights and interests of Member States in this process, and we'll go on like that in the follow-up of our work. Finally, I would like to say that many of the things that are in UNAT will have their follow-up in the future, and I hope that in the future other aspects will be considered in order to make the UN always more effective, responding to the needs of Member States and responding to the needs of the people we serve. I'd also like to guarantee to the distinguished co-chairs and to all member states that the secretariat will be 100% in support of your activities, not to interfere with the analysis of mandates or with the decisions related to mandates, but to provide you with information and the tools and the statistics and the elements that might be required for your work to be as effective as possible. And I want to congratulate the co-chairs and to congratulate member states in general because I believe that work done until now is an absolutely remarkable demonstration of the capacity of member states working together in the United Nations. Finally, I want to say that we will be entirely at your disposal at any time in all aspects and, on the other hand, fully respecting that there must be full guidance of Member States in general and strict decision by Member States in the areas that are Member States' competence. It is not our intention in any aspect to undermine what are the rights of Member States in order to make sure that our organization is able to move forward and to move forward with a total engagement of its membership. Thank you very much.
